title: The Christmas Walk: Splitting the Nucleus
subtitle: The discovery of nuclear fission — Rome, Berlin, Stockholm, Kungälv, Copenhagen, Paris, New York, Washington, 1934–1939
intro: For four years after 1934 the best laboratories in Europe bombarded uranium with neutrons and read the results the wrong way. Enrico Fermi's group in Rome believed they had made elements heavier than uranium; Otto Hahn, Lise Meitner and Fritz Strassmann in Berlin spent years mapping a growing family of supposed 'transuranes'; Irène Joliot-Curie in Paris found a substance that behaved stubbornly like lanthanum and could not explain it. A chemist, Ida Noddack, had suggested in print as early as 1934 that the nucleus might simply break into large pieces. Almost nobody took her up on it.

The answer arrived in the middle of a political catastrophe. Meitner, Austrian-born and of Jewish descent, lost the protection of her passport when Germany annexed Austria and slipped across the Dutch border on 13 July 1938. Five months later Hahn and Strassmann, still in Berlin, found barium — an element roughly half the weight of uranium — among their products. Hahn wrote to Meitner in Stockholm before he wrote to anyone else. Over Christmas, in the small Swedish town of Kungälv, Meitner and her nephew Otto Frisch worked out on a walk in the snow that the uranium nucleus, pictured as a wobbling liquid drop, had split in two and released an enormous quantity of energy.

This chapter is built almost entirely from dated letters, laboratory notebooks and the received and published dates of scientific papers rather than from diaries. That is where the record of this discovery lives: Hahn and Meitner wrote to each other every few days, and those letters — together with Hahn's and Meitner's pocket diaries and the notebook pages from Berlin and Copenhagen — establish who knew what, and when. Two of our eyes (Laura Fermi, Leó Szilárd) are known chiefly through later memoirs and recollections, and they are tagged that way. Because all of this material is modern and in copyright, the entries are digests in our own words; there are no quotations beyond one or two famous phrases.

Put the eyes side by side and a race appears that none of them fully saw at the time. Frisch told Niels Bohr in Copenhagen on 3 January 1939; Bohr carried the secret across the Atlantic and, though he meant to protect Meitner and Frisch's priority, the news slipped out at Princeton the day he landed. Within days of his announcement in Washington on 26 January, laboratories in New York, Washington, Baltimore, Berkeley and Paris had reproduced the effect. By March the Paris team of Frédéric Joliot, Hans von Halban and Lew Kowarski, and two groups at Columbia, had shown that each split released extra neutrons — the condition for a chain reaction. Szilárd, who had been afraid of exactly this since 1933, tried and failed to persuade physicists to stop publishing, and by August had Albert Einstein's signature on a letter to President Roosevelt.

The coda is the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, given in November 1945 to Hahn alone. Historians have argued over that decision ever since; the chapter reports their positions and the evidence they cite, not a verdict of its own.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Scientific priority here rests on the received or submitted dates printed with papers, the issue dates of journals, and the dates on letters; where those differ (for example Hahn and Strassmann's paper, submitted 22 December 1938 and carried in the Naturwissenschaften issue dated 6 January 1939), both are given in the claims ledger. Events in Europe and America on the same calendar day are separated by six hours of time difference, which matters for the scramble of late January 1939.

eyes.name: Lise Meitner
eyes.role: Physicist, 59–60; for thirty years Hahn's partner at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Chemistry, head of its physics section; from August 1938 a refugee guest at Manne Siegbahn's Nobel Institute in Stockholm
eyes.side: Austrian émigrée (Jewish descent, Protestant convert); exile in Sweden
eyes.where: Berlin-Dahlem until 13 July 1938; then Groningen, Copenhagen, Stockholm; Christmas 1938 in Kungälv
eyes.vantage_label: the exile who supplied the physics, by letter
eyes.authenticity: Her correspondence with Hahn and her pocket diaries survive in the Meitner Papers, Churchill Archives Centre, Cambridge, and have been used extensively by Ruth Lewin Sime and Roger Stuewer. Her diary-based account of the escape is summarized in Crawford, Sime and Walker (Physics Today, 1997). The letters are published in German editions; all digests here are paraphrases.
eyes.bio: Meitner had steered the Berlin uranium programme from its start in 1934 and was its physicist; when she fled she lost her laboratory, her salary and most of her standing. From Stockholm she followed Hahn's experiments by post and pressed him to check his results. Her angle is unique: she was inside the work and outside the country at the same time, and the decisive interpretation was hers and Frisch's.

sources.title: R. H. Stuewer, 'An Act of Creation: The Meitner-Frisch Interpretation of Nuclear Fission' (MPRL Proceedings 5, ch. 9, 2013)
E. Crawford, R. L. Sime, M. Walker, 'A Nobel Tale of Postwar Injustice', Physics Today, Sept 1997
BBC Science Focus: Lise Meitner, the nuclear pioneer who escaped the Nazis

eyes.name: Otto Hahn
eyes.role: Radiochemist, 59; director of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Chemistry, Berlin-Dahlem
eyes.where: Berlin-Dahlem; brief trip to Copenhagen in November 1938; interned at Farm Hall, England, in 1945

waypoints.label: Copenhagen, meets Meitner at Bohr's institute (Nov 1938)

eyes.vantage_label: the chemist at the bench who found barium
eyes.form: dated letters, laboratory notebook and pocket diary
eyes.authenticity: His letters to Meitner (originals largely in Cambridge) and the Berlin notebook labelled 'Chem-II', now with the apparatus at the Deutsches Museum, Munich, are the primary record. Hahn's later autobiographical writings (e.g. 1966) differ in emphasis from the contemporary letters, and historians have weighed them against each other.
eyes.bio: Hahn was the most skilled radiochemist of his generation and trusted his chemistry more than any physical theory. His letters show him certain of the chemistry and baffled by what it meant, turning first to Meitner for an explanation. His later account of the discovery as a purely chemical achievement is one of the reasons the credit question remains disputed.

sources.title: R. H. Stuewer, 'Bringing the news of fission to America', Physics Today, Oct 1985
Deutsches Museum: Hahn-Meitner-Strassmann table (Google Arts & Culture)
Linda Hall Library: Otto Hahn

eyes.name: Fritz (Friedrich Wilhelm) Strassmann
eyes.role: Analytical chemist, 36; Hahn's collaborator at the KWI for Chemistry, barred from habilitation after leaving the Nazi-aligned chemists' society
eyes.side: Germany (anti-Nazi; later Righteous Among the Nations)
eyes.form: laboratory notebook (shared with Hahn) and papers
eyes.authenticity: His contribution is visible in the shared Berlin notebook and in the co-authored papers of November 1938, 6 January 1939 and February 1939. His own reflections are later. Yad Vashem recognized him and his wife in 1985 for hiding Andrea Wolffenstein in their Berlin flat in 1943.
eyes.bio: Strassmann did much of the fine chemical separation; Chemistry World credits him with the barium-chloride carrier that gave cleaner crystals. Hahn always named him as co-author, but he was left out of the Nobel Prize and lived, in the phrase of Crawford, Sime and Walker, in Hahn's shadow. His is the view of the junior partner who did the work and was not consulted on the credit.

sources.title: Chemistry World: Fritz Strassmann, the principled chemist who discovered nuclear fission
Yad Vashem, Righteous Among the Nations database

eyes.name: Otto Robert Frisch
eyes.role: Physicist, 34; Meitner's nephew; refugee working at Bohr's Institute for Theoretical Physics, Copenhagen
eyes.where: Copenhagen; Christmas 1938 with Meitner at Kungälv

waypoints.label: Copenhagen: tells Bohr, runs the experiment (Jan 1939)

eyes.form: dated letters, laboratory notebook; memoir (written later)
eyes.authenticity: His letters to Meitner and Bohr of January 1939 survive (Bohr and Meitner archives) and are analysed by Stuewer. His memoir What Little I Remember (1979) is the source for the much-retold walk in the snow and Bohr's reaction; it was written forty years on and is flagged as memoir.
eyes.bio: Frisch did the arithmetic in Kungälv, chose the word 'fission' after asking a biologist colleague what splitting cells was called, and on 13 January 1939 became the first to see the fragments' pulses on an oscilloscope. He then delayed writing to Bohr for weeks, a lapse that nearly cost him and Meitner their priority. After 1940 he and Rudolf Peierls wrote the memorandum that set Britain's bomb project going.

sources.title: R. H. Stuewer, 'Bringing the news of fission to America', Physics Today, Oct 1985
APS News: This Month in Physics History — Meitner and Frisch

eyes.name: Niels Bohr
eyes.role: Physicist, 53; director of the Institute for Theoretical Physics, Copenhagen; Nobel laureate 1922
eyes.where: Copenhagen; at sea on the Drottningholm 7–16 January 1939; Princeton and Washington

waypoints.label: Gothenburg, sails on the Drottningholm (7 Jan)

eyes.vantage_label: the messenger who carried the news to America
eyes.authenticity: His letters to Frisch of 20 and 24 January and 3 February 1939 survive in the Niels Bohr Archive and are quoted in Stuewer (1985). His notes to Nature and the Physical Review carry received dates. Accounts of his remarks at the station and on board come from Frisch and Rosenfeld.
eyes.bio: Bohr grasped the idea at once in Copenhagen and spent his voyage working on it with Léon Rosenfeld. He tried hard to protect Meitner and Frisch's priority and was distressed when the story leaked and American groups rushed to confirm it. On board and in Princeton he reasoned that slow-neutron fission came from the rare isotope uranium-235, the insight that later shaped the whole bomb project.

sources.title: R. H. Stuewer, 'Bringing the news of fission to America', Physics Today, Oct 1985
AIP History: Nuclear fission timeline (Physics History Network)

eyes.name: Enrico Fermi
eyes.role: Physicist, 32–38; professor at Rome (Via Panisperna group); Nobel laureate 1938; from January 1939 at Columbia University
eyes.side: Italy, then émigré in the United States
eyes.where: Rome; Stockholm (Dec 1938); New York and Washington (1939)
eyes.vantage_label: the rival who started the race and misread the result
eyes.authenticity: His 1934 letters to Nature and La Ricerca Scientifica are the contemporary record; his Nobel lecture text was printed with a late note acknowledging the Berlin barium result. Personal detail comes mostly from Laura Fermi's memoir and later interviews with colleagues such as Emilio Segrè.
eyes.bio: Fermi's neutron programme opened the field in 1934 and won him the Nobel Prize for, among other things, the 'transuranic' elements that turned out to be fission products. He used the Stockholm trip to emigrate with his family. Within weeks of landing he was measuring fission and secondary neutrons at Columbia, and he became the most important builder of the chain reaction.

sources.title: E. Fermi, 'Possible Production of Elements of Atomic Number Higher than 92', Nature 133 (1934) — transcription
Los Alamos: Science earned Enrico Fermi a Nobel Prize and saved his Jewish family

eyes.name: Ida Noddack (née Tacke)
eyes.role: Chemist, 38; co-discoverer of rhenium (1925), working as an unpaid 'guest' alongside her husband Walter Noddack
eyes.where: Germany (Berlin circle of the Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt; the Noddacks moved to Freiburg in 1935)
eyes.vantage_label: the outside critic who proposed the answer and was ignored
eyes.authenticity: 'Über das Element 93', Angewandte Chemie 47 (1934), is the documentary record; her March 1939 letter to Naturwissenschaften and later recollections by Segrè and Hahn record the reception. Whether she sent reprints to Fermi is not documented; Segrè recalled that the Rome group saw the paper.
eyes.bio: Noddack argued that Fermi had not ruled out lighter elements, and that a heavy nucleus hit by neutrons might break into several large fragments that were isotopes of known elements. She did no experiment to test it and offered no physical mechanism, and the physicists of 1934 dismissed it. Her eye shows how an idea can be in print and still not be part of a field.

sources.title: Atomic Heritage Foundation: Ida Noddack
Seeking Scientific Revolutions: Ida Noddack — why the first proposal of fission was ignored

eyes.name: Irène Joliot-Curie
eyes.role: Physicist and chemist, 41; daughter of Marie Curie; Nobel laureate in Chemistry 1935 (with Frédéric Joliot); at the Institut du Radium, Paris
eyes.where: Institut du Radium, rue Pierre-Curie, Paris
eyes.vantage_label: the rival laboratory that came closest without seeing it
eyes.authenticity: Her work with Pavel (Paul) Savitch is recorded in their 1938 papers in Comptes rendus and the Journal de Physique; the reading of those results as an early sighting of fission comes from later historians (e.g. Radvanyi).
eyes.bio: In 1938 Irène Joliot-Curie and Savitch reported a 3.5-hour activity from irradiated uranium that behaved chemically like lanthanum — in hindsight, a fission product. Their result is what drove Hahn and Strassmann back to the bench in the autumn of 1938. Hers is the eye of the worker whose anomaly forced the answer into the open.

sources.title: AIP: Nuclear energy chronology 1896–1945
P. Radvanyi, Europhysics News 40/6 (2009)

eyes.name: Frédéric Joliot-Curie
eyes.role: Physicist, 38–39; professor at the Collège de France, leading a team with Hans von Halban and Lew Kowarski
eyes.where: Laboratoire de chimie nucléaire, Collège de France, Paris (and the Ivry laboratory)
eyes.vantage_label: the rival who won the secondary-neutron race
eyes.authenticity: His January 1939 recoil experiment and the March and April 1939 letters to Nature with Halban and Kowarski are the record; the patents filed on 1–3 May 1939 and the sealed note deposited with the Académie des Sciences after war broke out are described by Radvanyi.
eyes.bio: Joliot confirmed the splitting by physical means within days of reading Hahn's paper, then turned at once to the question that mattered: does each fission release more neutrons? His team answered yes, published, and refused Szilárd's pleas for secrecy. In June 1940 Halban and Kowarski carried the team's heavy water to England.

sources.title: P. Radvanyi, Europhysics News 40/6 (2009)
Halban, Joliot, Kowarski, 'Liberation of Neutrons in the Nuclear Explosion of Uranium', Nature 143, 470 (1939) — Scilit record

eyes.name: Leó Szilárd
eyes.role: Physicist, 40–41; Hungarian refugee without a regular post, working as a guest at Columbia University
eyes.side: Hungarian émigré in the United States
eyes.where: New York (King's Crown Hotel; Columbia); Long Island for the Einstein visits

waypoints.label: Nassau Point, Peconic, Einstein's summer house (July 1939)

eyes.vantage_label: the man who saw the bomb coming
eyes.authenticity: His 1939 letters and drafts survive in the Szilard Papers, UC San Diego (many digitized). His vivid account of the March 1939 experiment and of the Einstein visits comes from recollections dictated in the 1960s, published in Leo Szilard: His Version of the Facts (1978); treat those details as memoir.
eyes.bio: Szilárd had imagined a neutron chain reaction in London in 1933 and patented the idea. When fission was announced he tried to organize voluntary secrecy among physicists, then measured the secondary neutrons himself with Walter Zinn. When that failed to slow anyone down he turned to politics, and the Einstein letter was his doing.

sources.title: US DOE OpenNet: Leo Szilard (Manhattan Project history)
Szilard & Zinn, 'Instantaneous Emission of Fast Neutrons…', Phys. Rev. 55, 799 (1939) — record

eyes.name: Albert Einstein
eyes.role: Physicist, 60; at the Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton; summering at Nassau Point, Peconic, Long Island
eyes.side: German-born émigré in the United States
eyes.where: Old Grove Road, Nassau Point, Peconic, Long Island (summer 1939)
eyes.vantage_label: the famous name lent to the warning
eyes.language: English (drafted with Szilárd, partly from German)
eyes.authenticity: The signed letter dated 2 August 1939 survives at the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library; Atomic Heritage Foundation reproduces it. Einstein's part in drafting is documented in Szilárd's papers; his own later statements about it are retrospective.
eyes.bio: Einstein had no part in the fission work and had doubted that nuclear energy could be released in practice. He understood Szilárd's argument quickly once it was put to him and agreed to sign. His eye is that of the outsider whose authority, not expertise, was needed.

sources.title: Atomic Heritage Foundation: Einstein-Szilard Letter (text)
Atomic Heritage Foundation: Einstein Letter, 1939

eyes.name: Eugene (Jenő) Wigner
eyes.role: Physicist, 36–37; professor at Princeton; Szilárd's friend and fellow Hungarian
eyes.side: Hungarian émigré in the United States
eyes.where: Princeton; drove Szilárd to Einstein on Long Island in July 1939

waypoints.label: Peconic, with Szilárd to Einstein (16 July 1939)

eyes.authenticity: His role is documented in Szilárd's papers and recalled in his own later memoir (The Recollections of Eugene P. Wigner, 1992). Edward Teller, who drove Szilárd on the second visit, gave his account in later memoirs; both are retrospective.
eyes.bio: Wigner was at Princeton when Bohr's news arrived and passed it to Szilárd, who was laid up in bed. In July 1939 he drove the non-driving Szilárd out to Long Island to find Einstein. He stands for the small circle of Hungarian émigrés who pushed the warning to Washington.

sources.title: US DOE OpenNet: Leo Szilard
AIP History: Nuclear fission timeline

eyes.name: Laura Fermi (née Capon)
eyes.role: Writer, 31; Enrico Fermi's wife, from a Jewish Roman family threatened by Italy's 1938 racial laws
eyes.side: Italy, then émigrée in the United States
eyes.where: Rome; Stockholm (Dec 1938); New York and Leonia, New Jersey (1939)
eyes.vantage_label: the family's eye on the physicists
eyes.authenticity: Atoms in the Family: My Life with Enrico Fermi (1954) was written fifteen years after the events, partly from memory; it is a lively but not contemporaneous source and is flagged here as memoir.
eyes.bio: Laura Fermi saw the discovery from the dinner table and the dockside rather than the laboratory. Her memoir records the strain of the racial laws, the Nobel Prize used as an escape route, and the physicists' talk in New York as fission broke. She is the only eye here who was not a scientist.

sources.title: Atomic Heritage Foundation: Laura Fermi

entries.headline: Rome announces a possible element heavier than uranium
entries.digest: Fermi's letter to Nature reports that his group has made forty-seven of sixty-eight elements radioactive by neutron bombardment. Uranium yields several activities, one of about thirteen minutes that his chemical tests separate from uranium and from every heavy element down to lead. He suggests it may be element 93, though he says plainly that the chemical evidence is weak and a firm conclusion premature. The caution was lost in the excitement; Italian newspapers hailed a new element.
entries.source_note: Nature 133, 898–899 (1934); transcription at chemteam.info. Issue date from the Nature volume sequence.

entries.headline: A chemist suggests the nucleus might break apart
entries.digest: In 'Über das Element 93' Ida Noddack faults Fermi's chemistry: he had not checked the products against all the lighter elements, so he could not claim element 93. She goes further and suggests that under neutron bombardment a heavy nucleus might break into several large fragments, isotopes of known elements far from uranium in the periodic table. The paper offers no experiment and no physics; the physicists who saw it set it aside.
entries.source_note: Angewandte Chemie 47 (1934); AHF profile; Seeking Scientific Revolutions essay. Month as conventionally cited; issue day not checked.

entries.headline: Paraffin slows the neutrons and boosts the effect
entries.digest: Fermi's group finds that neutrons passed through paraffin wax or water become far more effective at making elements radioactive; slowed by collisions with hydrogen, they linger near nuclei and are captured. The slow-neutron technique becomes the standard tool in Rome, Berlin and Paris, and it is the method by which uranium will eventually be split. The team patents the process.
entries.source_note: Date as given in standard Fermi biographies; not re-checked in a primary source this session.

entries.headline: Meitner leaves Berlin with ten marks and a borrowed ring
entries.digest: After a last day at the institute spent working as if nothing were wrong, Meitner leaves Berlin by train with the Dutch physicist Dirk Coster, carrying two small suitcases, ten marks and a diamond ring Hahn had given her from his mother's estate for an emergency. Her Austrian passport is no longer valid. At the Dutch border a patrol takes the papers away for anxious minutes and returns them without a word, and she reaches Groningen that evening. Her pocket diary records the shock of being cast out of the place that had been her life.
entries.source_note: Crawford, Sime & Walker (1997), diary-based account; BBC Science Focus; APS News (ten marks, ring).

entries.headline: A coded telegram: the baby has arrived
entries.digest: Hahn had helped plan the escape and spent the anxious hours in Berlin. Coster's telegram from Groningen, worded as if announcing a birth, tells him Meitner is safe across the border. Hahn is left running the uranium work with Strassmann, without the physicist who had steered it.
entries.source_note: BBC Science Focus account of the coded telegram; Stuewer (2013) for the date of the escape.

entries.headline: A desk without a laboratory in Stockholm
entries.digest: After a fortnight in Groningen and a stay with the Bohrs in Copenhagen, Meitner reaches Stockholm and a place at Manne Siegbahn's new Nobel Institute. She has a room and a small stipend but almost no equipment or assistants, and little welcome. Her letters to Hahn soon fill with questions about the Berlin uranium results.
entries.source_note: Route from Stuewer (2013) and SKBL; arrival date as given in Sime's biography, not re-checked this session.

entries.headline: Paris finds a uranium product that acts like lanthanum
entries.digest: Irène Joliot-Curie and Pavel Savitch report that one activity from neutron-irradiated uranium, with a half-life of about 3.5 hours, behaves chemically like lanthanum, element 57. They cannot reconcile this with any known transformation and cautiously interpret it within the transuranic picture. Hahn is sceptical of their chemistry, but the anomaly sends him and Strassmann back to check their own radium-like products.
entries.source_note: AIP chronology dates the lanthanum-like finding to August 1938; Radvanyi (2009) on the Curie-Savitch approach.

entries.headline: The Stockholm phone call becomes an escape route
entries.digest: Laura Fermi later recalled the morning call from Stockholm confirming the Nobel Prize, which came as Italy's racial laws closed in on her Jewish family. The couple had already decided to leave Italy; the prize gives them a reason to travel with their children and money waiting abroad. They tell the authorities they will be away for a few months.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (1985) gives the date of the Nobel call; Atoms in the Family (1954) for her recollection; AHF profile for the 'six months' cover story.

entries.headline: A quiet meeting with Meitner in Copenhagen
entries.digest: Hahn travels to Copenhagen to lecture and meets Meitner, who has come over from Stockholm, at Bohr's institute. She tells him she does not believe the Berlin claim that radium isotopes are being formed and urges him and Strassmann to test it again with greater care. Hahn later played the meeting down; Meitner's supporters treat it as evidence of her continuing role in the experiments.
entries.source_note: Crawford, Sime & Walker (1997) place the meeting in November 1938; the exact day (often given as 13 November) not re-checked.

entries.headline: The Fermis leave Rome with no plan to return
entries.digest: Laura Fermi recalled boarding the train north with Enrico, their two small children and a nursemaid, carrying only what a family visiting Stockholm might plausibly carry. She remembered the fear of a last-minute passport check and the feeling of leaving her parents behind in a country turning against them.
entries.source_note: Atoms in the Family (1954); AHF profile gives December 1938. Exact day from her memoir, not re-checked.

entries.headline: A Nobel lecture on elements that do not exist
entries.digest: Fermi receives the Nobel Prize in Physics for his neutron work and lectures on artificial radioactivity, describing the transuranic elements 93 and 94 that his group believed it had made. A week later Berlin's barium result would undercut that part of the lecture; when it was printed Fermi added a note saying the Hahn–Strassmann findings required the transuranic results to be re-examined. The printed lecture does not mention Noddack.
entries.source_note: Seeking Scientific Revolutions essay (lecture date, footnote); Nobel Foundation.

entries.headline: The 'radium' will not separate from barium
entries.digest: Working through the week with Hahn, Strassmann runs the decisive fractional crystallizations: the supposed radium isotopes from irradiated uranium stay with the barium carrier every time and cannot be separated from it. The notebook labelled 'Chem-II', now in the Deutsches Museum, holds the record. The only chemical conclusion is that the product is barium, and neither chemist yet knows what that means physically.
entries.source_note: SRF (17 December 1938 as the discovery date); Deutsches Museum notebook 'Chem-II'; Chemistry World on Strassmann's carrier technique.

entries.headline: Hahn writes to Meitner first: it is barium
entries.digest: At about eleven at night Hahn writes to Meitner that their radium isotopes behave like barium, that he and Strassmann keep reaching this dreadful conclusion, and that they have told no one else. He knows that uranium cannot simply burst into barium by any known physics and asks her whether she can find some fantastic explanation. He wants an answer before he publishes.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (1985), 'Bringing the news of fission to America', dating the letter to 11 pm on 19 Dec; Chemistry World on its content.

entries.headline: Meitner: astonishing, but physics has surprised us before
entries.digest: Meitner replies that a slow-neutron reaction leading to barium is very hard to accept, and asks Hahn whether he is absolutely certain of the chemistry. But she does not dismiss it: nuclear physics has produced so many surprises that she cannot say it is impossible. Hahn confirms the result in a letter the same day.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (1985); Chemistry World on the content of her reply.

entries.headline: The barium paper goes to Naturwissenschaften
entries.digest: Without waiting for Meitner's interpretation, Hahn and Strassmann send their paper to Die Naturwissenschaften, whose editor Paul Rosbaud agrees to rush it into print. As chemists they state that the product is barium; as 'nuclear chemists' close to physics they say they hesitate to take a step so contrary to all previous experience. Meitner's name is not on it — a political impossibility in Berlin, and a fact that later shaped the credit dispute.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (1985) gives submission 22 Dec 1938; AIP chronology gives publication 6 Jan 1939.

entries.headline: On a walk in the snow, the drop splits
entries.digest: Meitner, who had left Stockholm on the 23rd to spend Christmas with friends at Kungälv, shows her nephew Hahn's letter at breakfast. On a walk through the snowy woods, Frisch on skis and Meitner on foot, they sit on a tree trunk and work it through: if the nucleus is a liquid drop whose surface tension is nearly cancelled by electrical repulsion, a captured neutron could set it wobbling until it pinches into two. Meitner remembers the mass-defect rule and reckons the released energy at about 200 million electron volts — just what the two charged fragments would gain flying apart.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (2013): meeting 'probably on the morning of 24 December'; Stuewer (1985) for Meitner's 23 Dec departure; details of the walk from Frisch's later memoir.

entries.headline: Frisch arrives with his own experiment, and is diverted
entries.digest: Frisch had come from Copenhagen meaning to talk about a magnetic experiment of his own, but his aunt would not listen until he had read Hahn's letter. In his later telling he at first suspected a mistake, until Meitner insisted that Hahn was too good a chemist to be wrong. They worked out the numbers on scraps of paper; the two reasonings, chemistry and the liquid drop, agreed.
entries.source_note: Frisch, What Little I Remember (1979), memoir; Stuewer (2013) on the date.

entries.headline: Hahn floats a barium-masurium splitting as a 'fantasy'
entries.digest: Still unsure of the physics, Hahn writes that if uranium gives barium, perhaps the other piece is masurium (element 43, now technetium), so the numbers would add up to uranium's 92 protons. He frames it half-jokingly as a speculation he would not dare print. His letter crosses with Meitner's, which is already moving the same way.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (1985).

entries.headline: She and Frisch have been racking their brains
entries.digest: Meitner writes to Hahn that she and Frisch have been puzzling over the results all through the holiday, and that the energetics now look possible. She does not yet send the full liquid-drop argument but makes clear that a physical picture is taking shape.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (1985).

entries.headline: Back in Stockholm: it is energetically possible
entries.digest: Having read the manuscript Hahn sent her on 30 December, Meitner writes from Stockholm that it may be energetically possible for a heavy nucleus to break apart. Frisch returns to Copenhagen the same day. The interpretation now exists on paper in two cities, but has not been published.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (1985); Stuewer (2013) for the return dates.

entries.headline: Landing in New York as émigrés
entries.digest: The Fermi family arrive in New York from Europe. In her memoir Laura Fermi remembered Enrico remarking, as they passed the Statue of Liberty, that they had founded the American branch of the family. Fermi takes up a post at Columbia University; within three weeks the fission news will reach him there.
entries.source_note: AHF Laura Fermi profile (arrival 2 January 1939); remark from Atoms in the Family (memoir).

entries.headline: Frisch tells Bohr, who agrees at once
entries.digest: Frisch puts the idea to Bohr, who is packing for America. In Frisch's recollection Bohr struck his forehead and exclaimed at how blind everyone had been, then asked whether they had written it up. That evening Frisch writes to Meitner that Bohr fully agrees and has promised to say nothing until their note is out.
entries.quote: Oh what idiots we all have been!
entries.source_note: Stuewer (1985, 2013) for the date and Frisch's letter to Meitner; Bohr's exclamation from Frisch's memoir (1979), widely quoted.

entries.headline: The barium paper appears in print
entries.digest: Hahn and Strassmann's paper on alkaline-earth metals from neutron-irradiated uranium appears in Die Naturwissenschaften. It reports barium with chemical certainty but stops short of saying the nucleus has split. Read in Paris, Copenhagen and soon America, it sets off the race; Strassmann later recalled that the possible consequences frightened him.
entries.source_note: AIP chronology (6 Jan publication); Stuewer (1985) notes it reached readers around 8 Jan; SRF on Strassmann's later feelings.

entries.headline: Bohr sails with two pages and a promise
entries.digest: Frisch hands Bohr two pages of the draft note at the station as he leaves for the boat. Bohr sails from Gothenburg on the Drottningholm with his son Erik and his collaborator Léon Rosenfeld, and spends the voyage at a blackboard in his cabin working out the theory of the splitting drop. He intends to keep the news quiet until the Meitner–Frisch note is published.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (1985).

entries.headline: Fragments on the oscilloscope in the small hours
entries.digest: Using an ionization chamber lined with uranium and an amplifier, Frisch looks for the huge pulses that fission fragments should produce. Shortly after three in the morning they appear — far larger than anything alpha particles could make — and they vanish when the neutron source is removed. He spends the next days confirming it, the first physical proof that the nucleus splits.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (2013) for the time; Stuewer (1985) for the confirmation over three days.

entries.headline: Two notes go to Nature; the word 'fission' is born
entries.digest: After long-distance telephone calls between Stockholm and Copenhagen, Meitner and Frisch's note on the disintegration of uranium by neutrons is sent to Nature, together with Frisch's separate note on the physical evidence. Frisch had borrowed the biologists' word for cell division, so the process gets the name it still has. Neither author knows that in New York the secret is about to slip.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (1985) gives submission of both notes on 16 Jan; APS News and Radvanyi on the naming.

entries.headline: The ship docks and the news escapes
entries.digest: The Drottningholm docks in New York, where John Wheeler and the Fermis meet the party. Bohr stays in the city; Rosenfeld goes on to Princeton with Wheeler and, not realizing he was meant to keep silent, describes the splitting of uranium at the physics journal club that evening. Bohr is dismayed when he learns, and writes anxiously to Frisch over the following week to find out whether the Nature note has gone in.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (1985): docking, Rosenfeld's journal-club talk, Bohr's letters of 20 and 24 Jan.

entries.headline: Szilárd hears and fears a chain reaction
entries.digest: Visiting Wigner in Princeton, where Szilárd is laid up with a cold, he learns of the Hahn–Strassmann result and Bohr's news. He sees at once that if each split also frees neutrons, the chain reaction he had imagined in London in 1933 becomes possible — and that Germany has the discovery. He begins writing to colleagues urging that further results be kept out of print.
entries.source_note: DOE OpenNet (heard via Wigner; secrecy campaign); AIP timeline (campaign begins Jan 1939); details from Szilárd's later recollections.

entries.headline: Columbia sees the pulses the night before Washington
entries.digest: Bohr stops at Columbia on his way to Washington. That evening, in the basement of Pupin Hall, Herbert Anderson with John Dunning's group — Fermi having already left for the conference — records the large ionization pulses of fission fragments, the first confirmation in America. Fermi had suggested the experiment and also proposed that neutrons might be emitted in the process.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (1985); AIP chronology credits Dunning, Slack and Booth at Columbia (dated 26 Jan there).

entries.headline: Bohr announces fission; physicists run for their labs
entries.digest: At the Fifth Washington Conference on Theoretical Physics, Bohr — with Fermi joining in — describes the Hahn–Strassmann result and the Meitner–Frisch interpretation. Several listeners leave before the session ends to set up the experiment. Bohr is careful to credit Meitner and Frisch, but news reports the next day spread the story as an American sensation.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (1985, 2013); AIP fission timeline.

entries.headline: Fermi talks of neutrons and a chain reaction
entries.digest: Speaking after Bohr, Fermi raises the possibility that the splitting nucleus might emit neutrons, which could in turn split other nuclei. The remark turns the discussion from a curiosity of nuclear physics to a possible source of energy. Within two days groups at the Carnegie Institution and Johns Hopkins had reproduced fission, and showed it to Bohr and Fermi on the night of the 28th.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (1985): Roberts's group at the Carnegie Institution and Fowler and Dodson at Johns Hopkins confirm on 28 Jan.

entries.headline: Paris catches the recoiling fragments
entries.digest: Reading the Hahn–Strassmann paper, Joliot designs a simple test: fragments flung out of a uranium layer should travel a short distance and deposit radioactivity on a nearby surface. They do, and he reports a physical proof of the splitting independently of Frisch, followed by cloud-chamber pictures of the tracks. He turns his team at once to counting neutrons.
entries.source_note: Radvanyi (2009): 'end of January 1939'; AIP chronology lists Joliot's verification under 26 Jan.

entries.headline: The lanthanum puzzle explained, by others
entries.digest: With fission confirmed, Irène Joliot-Curie and Savitch's 3.5-hour 'lanthanum-like' substance falls into place as a genuine fission product. Their work had prompted the Berlin re-examination, but the decisive identification belonged to Hahn and Strassmann. The Paris laboratory joins the international rush to characterize the fragments.
entries.source_note: AIP chronology and Radvanyi (2009); no dated document of Irène's reaction found this session — this entry summarizes the scientific situation.

entries.headline: A plea to Paris: please don't publish
entries.digest: Szilárd writes to Joliot proposing that physicists in America, Britain and France hold back any results on neutron emission from fission, so as not to help Germany. Fermi, at Columbia, thinks secrecy is wrong and the danger remote; Teller and Wigner side with Szilárd. Joliot does not agree to hold back.
entries.source_note: DOE OpenNet (Szilárd urged Joliot to delay publication; Fermi opposed secrecy); exact date of the letter not verified this session.

entries.headline: The interpretation is published under her own name
entries.digest: Meitner and Frisch's note appears in Nature, explaining the barium result as the splitting of the uranium nucleus into two roughly equal parts with a release of about 200 million electron volts. Frisch's experimental note follows on 18 February and Bohr's on 25 February. By then dozens of laboratories have repeated the effect, and Meitner, far from her old apparatus, writes to friends that she feels left behind.
entries.source_note: Stuewer (1985) for the Nature issue dates; Nature 143, 239–240. Her feeling of isolation as summarized by Sime; not re-checked letter by letter.

entries.headline: Flashes on the screen, and then the switch off
entries.digest: With Walter Zinn and a borrowed radium-beryllium source, Szilárd looks for fast neutrons coming out of uranium bombarded with slow ones. When they turn the apparatus on, the screen shows the flashes they were looking for. In his later account Szilárd went home that night certain that the world was headed for great trouble.
entries.source_note: AIP chronology (Columbia experiments completed by 15 March); day and his reaction from Szilárd's later recollections (memoir).

entries.headline: Paris sends Nature the secondary neutrons
entries.digest: Joliot, Halban and Kowarski complete their measurement showing that neutrons are freed when uranium splits, and send a letter to Nature, which prints it in the issue of 18 March. It is the first published evidence that a chain reaction might be possible. The Columbia groups' parallel papers go to the Physical Review a week later.
entries.source_note: AIP chronology (8 March); Nature 143, 470–471 (1939), Scilit record. Issue date of 18 March from the volume sequence.

entries.headline: Noddack reminds everyone she said it first
entries.digest: Ida Noddack publishes a letter in Die Naturwissenschaften pointing out that her 1934 paper had already raised the possibility that uranium breaks into large fragments, and criticizing Hahn and Strassmann for not citing it. The editors print a response on Hahn and Strassmann's behalf. The exchange settles nothing, and her priority claim stays on the margins for decades.
entries.source_note: Seeking Scientific Revolutions essay (March 1939 letter and editorial response).

entries.headline: Between two and three neutrons per split
entries.digest: The Paris team sends a second letter to Nature estimating that each fission releases on average between three and four neutrons (later revised downward to about two and a half). The Columbia groups come to a similar figure independently. The chain reaction now looks a matter of engineering, and on 1–3 May the team files patents on nuclear energy and explosives through France's national research fund.
entries.source_note: AIP chronology (April: two or three neutrons per fission); Radvanyi (2009) for the patents of 1–3 May 1939; submission day not verified.

entries.headline: Lost on Long Island, looking for Einstein
entries.digest: Wigner drives Szilárd out to Long Island to see Einstein at his rented summer house; after getting lost they find it by asking a boy in the street. Their first idea is to warn Belgium, through Einstein's acquaintance with the Queen Mother, to keep the uranium of the Belgian Congo out of German hands. Einstein grasps the chain-reaction argument quickly and agrees to help; Wigner helps take down a draft letter in German.
entries.source_note: AIP timeline and DOE OpenNet give 16 July; other sources give 12 July. Details from Szilárd's and Wigner's later recollections.

entries.headline: Einstein hears the argument for the first time
entries.digest: Einstein, who had long doubted that atomic energy could be released, listens to Szilárd explain secondary neutrons and a chain in a mass of uranium, and is said to have remarked that he had never thought of it. He agrees to lend his name to a warning. The question becomes whom to warn and through what channel.
entries.source_note: AIP timeline (visit date); Einstein's remark is reported in Szilárd's recollections, not in a contemporary document.

entries.headline: Back to Einstein, with Teller driving
entries.digest: On the advice of the economist Alexander Sachs, who has access to Roosevelt, the plan has grown into a letter to the President. Edward Teller drives Szilárd to Long Island for a second visit, at which the letter is redrafted. Szilárd then prepares a long and a short version for Einstein to choose between.
entries.source_note: AHF 'Einstein Letter, 1939' (30 July, Teller drove; final draft to Sachs 15 August).

entries.place: Old Grove Road, Nassau Point, Peconic
entries.headline: The signed letter to Roosevelt
entries.digest: Einstein signs the letter, dated from Peconic, telling the President that recent work by Fermi and Szilárd makes a chain reaction in uranium likely and that bombs of unprecedented power might follow. It urges contact between the government and the physicists, securing uranium ore, and funding for experiments, and notes that Germany has stopped the sale of uranium from occupied Czechoslovakia. Szilárd passes it to Sachs in mid-August; the war in Europe begins before it is delivered.
entries.source_note: Text reproduced by Atomic Heritage Foundation; AHF and AIP timeline for the 2 August date.

entries.headline: Sachs reads the warning to the President
entries.digest: Alexander Sachs finally sees Roosevelt and, rather than handing over the letter, reads and summarizes it with his own covering arguments. Roosevelt orders action, and an Advisory Committee on Uranium under Lyman Briggs meets on 21 October, with Szilárd, Wigner and Teller present. Einstein, not in the room, learns of the outcome by letter.
entries.source_note: AHF 'Einstein Letter, 1939'; AIP timeline (11 and 21 October).

entries.headline: News of the Nobel reaches an interned Hahn
entries.digest: Held with other German nuclear scientists at Farm Hall, Hahn learns from the newspaper that the Royal Swedish Academy has given him the 1944 chemistry prize for the discovery of fission; the vote had come on 15 November, by a narrow majority. Meitner and Strassmann are not included. Crawford, Sime and Walker later argued that the award reflected disciplinary bias and wartime isolation in the committees; defenders of the decision stressed the chemical character of the identification. The book reports both positions.
entries.source_note: Crawford, Sime & Walker (1997) for the November 1945 decision and their arguments; day of Hahn learning at Farm Hall from the Farm Hall transcripts as usually cited, not re-checked.

A bombarded heavy nucleus might break into several large fragments
A 3.5-hour uranium product behaves chemically like lanthanum
claims.evidence: Curie & Savitch, Comptes rendus / Journal de Physique 1938; AIP chronology

claims.claim: Supposed radium isotopes cannot be separated from barium carrier
Barium is among the products; asks Meitner for an explanation
claims.evidence: Hahn to Meitner; Stuewer, Physics Today 1985

claims.claim: Hahn & Strassmann report alkaline-earth (barium) products from uranium
Breaking of the heavy nucleus may be energetically possible
Bohr told of the splitting interpretation; agrees, promises discretion

claims.evidence: Die Naturwissenschaften 27, issue dated 6 Jan 1939; AIP chronology

claims.claim: Ionization pulses of fission fragments observed
Meitner–Frisch interpretation ('fission') and Frisch's evidence sent to Nature

claims.evidence: Fifth Washington Conference on Theoretical Physics; Stuewer 1985; AIP

claims.claim: Neutrons are liberated in uranium fission
claims.evidence: Halban, Joliot, Kowarski, Nature 143, 470 (issue of 18 March); AIP chronology

claims.claim: Chain reaction in uranium may make possible bombs of a new type
claims.evidence: Einstein to Roosevelt, FDR Library; AHF

claims.claim: Warning delivered to Roosevelt via Sachs

convergences.label: Meitner crosses the Dutch border
convergences.note: The same day seen from the train and from Berlin: Meitner records loss and expulsion; Hahn waits for a coded telegram and is left with the experiment but without its physicist.

convergences.label: Barium: Hahn's letter, Meitner's reply, the paper submitted (19–22 Dec)
convergences.note: In four days the chemistry goes from notebook to letter to journal. The Berlin pair are sure of the chemistry and unsure of the meaning; Meitner in Stockholm is doubtful of the chemistry and open to the physics. The paper is submitted before her interpretation arrives.

convergences.label: The Kungälv walk
convergences.note: As Meitner and Frisch reason out the liquid-drop split, Hahn in Berlin is circling the same answer by arithmetic (his barium-masurium letter of the 28th); their letters cross.

convergences.label: Copenhagen to the Atlantic (3–7 Jan)
convergences.note: In one week Frisch convinces Bohr, the Berlin paper reaches readers, Bohr sails, and in New York the newly arrived Fermis are settling in without knowing what is coming toward them.

convergences.label: Same day, two continents
convergences.note: In Scandinavia the Nature notes are posted to secure priority; that evening in Princeton Rosenfeld unknowingly gives the news away. Bohr spends the following week anxious about whether the notes have gone in.

convergences.label: The Washington conference and the rush to replicate (25–30 Jan)
convergences.note: Columbia, Washington, Baltimore and Paris confirm fission within days; Fermi talks of neutrons and chain reactions in public while Szilárd begins urging silence.

convergences.label: The secondary-neutron race (March 1939)
convergences.note: Paris publishes, Columbia measures the same thing, Szilárd pleads for secrecy and is refused — and in Germany Noddack is arguing about 1934.

convergences.label: The drive to Peconic
convergences.note: The only meeting in the chapter recorded from three sides, all of them in later recollection: the friend who drove, the man with the argument, and the man whose name would carry it.

ties.note: Partners in Berlin for thirty years; after July 1938 their collaboration continued by letter and in one meeting in Copenhagen.
Aunt and nephew; they worked out the interpretation together at Kungälv and co-wrote the Nature note.
Co-authors at the bench; Hahn always named Strassmann as co-discoverer but alone received the Nobel Prize.
Frisch worked at Bohr's institute and told him the news on 3 January 1939; Bohr then carried it to America.
Noddack's 1934 paper criticized Fermi's element 93 claim; Segrè recalled that the Rome group saw it but did not pursue it.
Curie and Savitch's lanthanum-like activity, which Hahn doubted, drove the Berlin re-examination that found barium.
Husband and wife and joint Nobel laureates of 1935, by 1939 leading separate laboratories in Paris.
Not enemies but opposite views on secrecy: Szilárd begged Paris to hold back neutron results; Joliot published.
Colleagues at Columbia who measured secondary neutrons in parallel and disagreed over whether to publish.
Old friends from Berlin (they had patented a refrigerator together); Szilárd drafted the 1939 letter Einstein signed.
Fellow Hungarians; Wigner relayed the fission news to Szilárd and drove him to Einstein.
Wife and husband; her memoir is the main family account of the emigration that coincided with the discovery.
They met at the New York dock and announced fission together in Washington.

threads_out.note: Irène Joliot-Curie, Marie Curie's daughter, worked at the Institut du Radium her mother built, and the radium-beryllium and polonium neutron sources used throughout this race descend from the Curies' radioactive chemistry. Hahn's task in 1938 was the classic Curie method: fractional crystallization to separate radium from barium.

The Einstein–Szilárd letter was delivered six weeks after Germany invaded Poland; in June 1940 Halban and Kowarski fled France for England with the Paris team's heavy water, and Frisch and Peierls's 1940 memorandum launched Britain's bomb work.

The chain reaction measured in Paris and New York in March 1939 led through the Manhattan Project to the bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki; Hahn heard of Hiroshima while interned at Farm Hall, three months before learning of his Nobel Prize.
After the war Szilárd left physics for biology, partly in reaction to the bomb, and became an influential figure in the early molecular biology community from which the double-helix work emerged.
